items.title: Scoring four forecasts
items.prose: A model's misses on four test days were 1, −1, 2 and 0 (in %).
items.question: What is the test mean squared error?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square each miss, then average.

byKey.mae: That is the mean absolute error. Square the misses first.
byKey.signed: The signed misses cancel. Square them first.
byKey.sum: That is the sum of squares. Divide by the 4 days.

explain.text: The squared misses are 1, 1, 4 and 0, which average to 1.5. The day that missed by 2 carries two thirds of it.

items.title: Three neighbours on a line
items.prose: Training days have signal $x$ = 1, 2, 4, 7 and next-day returns $y$ = 3, 5, 4, 10. Today's signal is $x_0 = 3$.
items.question: What does 3-NN forecast?

widget.accept: 4: the nearest are $x = 2$ and $x = 4$ (distance 1) and $x = 1$ (distance 2), so $(5 + 4 + 3)/3$.
widget.label: Forecast

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Measure each day's distance from 3, then average the three nearest targets.

byKey.two: That averages only two neighbours. $k = 3$ needs one more: $x = 1$, at distance 2.
byKey.all: That averages all four days, which is $k = 4$.
byKey.wrong3: You took $x = 7$, at distance 4. The day at $x = 1$ is nearer.

explain.text: Distances from 3 are 2, 1, 1 and 4. The three nearest days have targets 3, 5 and 4, so the forecast is 4.

items.title: Adding a degree
items.prose: A degree-6 polynomial fitted by least squares has training MSE 0.30 and test MSE 0.42. You refit the same training rows at degree 7.
items.question: Which statement must hold?

options.text: Degree 7's training MSE is at most 0.30
Degree 7's test MSE is at most 0.42
options.why: Nothing ties the test error to the fit. It may rise or fall.
Only the training error is forced down; the test rows took no part in the fit.
Degree 7 can copy the degree-6 curve with a zero top coefficient, so it cannot do worse on the training rows.

feedback.correct: Nested models: training error cannot rise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which error the least squares search minimises.

explain.text: Every degree-6 polynomial is a degree-7 one with top coefficient 0, so least squares at degree 7 does at least as well on the training rows. The test MSE is free to go either way.

items.title: Three parts
items.prose: At one point, refits on 400 training sets give predictions with mean 1.8 and standard deviation 0.5. The true value there is 2.0, and the noise variance is 0.2.
items.question: What is the expected test error at that point?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the bias and the sd, then add the noise variance.

byKey.nosq: You added bias and sd without squaring. Both enter squared.
byKey.nonoise: You left out the noise. A new day brings it whatever the model.
byKey.sdnotsq: You squared the bias but not the sd.

explain.text: Bias $1.8 - 2.0 = -0.2$ squares to 0.04, the sd squares to 0.25, and the noise adds 0.2: 0.49.

items.title: Ten years of days
items.prose: You have daily features and next-day returns from 2015 to 2024 and want one honest test score.
items.question: Which split gives it?

options.text: Train on 2015 to 2022, test on 2023 and 2024
Shuffle all days, train on 80% and test on 20%
options.why: A shuffle puts later days into training, so the model learns from the future of its own test days.

options.text: Train on odd-numbered days, test on even ones
options.why: Neighbouring days share news and volatility, so the test days are near-copies of training days.

options.text: Train and test on all ten years, for the most data
options.why: Scoring on training rows gives training error, which flatters the model.

feedback.correct: Train on the past, test on what came after.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The test days must come after every training day.

explain.text: Live, a model is always fitted on the past and used on the future. A time-ordered split is the only one that copies that.

items.title: Four models averaged
items.prose: Four forecasting models each have bias² 0.10 and variance 0.60, and their errors are independent. The noise variance is 0.50. You average their forecasts.
items.question: What is the expected test error of the average?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Averaging divides only the variance by the number of models.

byKey.one: That is a single model's error.
byKey.allquarter: You divided all three parts by 4. Bias and noise do not average away.
byKey.biasq: You divided the bias by 4 as well. Copies of a biased model share the bias.

explain.text: Averaging four independent forecasts divides their variance by four: 0.60 becomes 0.15. Bias stays at 0.10 and the noise at 0.50, so the total falls from 1.20 to 0.75.

items.title: Significant but useless
items.prose: A regression of a fund's monthly return on the same month's value factor gives $t = 6.2$ and $R^2 = 0.35$ over 10 years. Used to forecast next month from this month's factor, its test MSE equals the mean forecast's.
items.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: The factor explains returns in the same month but does not predict the next month
The two results contradict each other, so one is wrong
options.why: They answer different questions: same-month explanation and next-month prediction.

options.text: The high $t$ means the forecast should work; the test is unlucky
options.why: A $t$ statistic measures the same-month coefficient. The forecast is judged on new months.

options.text: With $R^2 = 0.35$ the forecast must beat the mean
options.why: In-sample $R^2$ on the same month says nothing about next month.

feedback.correct: Explaining and predicting are different questions.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check which month each result is about.

explain.text: The same-month loading is real and significant: that is inference. The lagged forecast has no edge: that is prediction, judged on test error. Both can be true at once.

items.title: Distance in mixed units
items.prose: A $k$-NN model uses two raw features: daily volatility in per cent (sd 0.8) and traded value in £ millions (sd 50).
items.question: Before computing distances, what should you do?

options.text: Divide each feature by its standard deviation (after centring)

options.why: Euclidean distance adds raw squared gaps, so the £ column swamps the per cent one.
Logs change shapes but not the gap in scale between per cent and £ millions.

options.text: Drop the volatility feature, since it is small
options.why: It is small only in its units. Scaled, it may matter as much as traded value.

feedback.correct: Standardise, so both features count on the same scale.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which feature dominates a raw distance.

explain.text: A typical traded-value gap of £50m squares to 2,500; a volatility gap of 0.8 squares to 0.64. Standardising puts both on a scale of one standard deviation.
